metadata.title: The Regression Problem
metadata.purpose: STEM & AI Architecture, Week 7 — why AI pipelines degrade silently, why you test the deterministic guardrails rather than the model's words, and how a CI gate turns 'it probably still works' into something the repository enforces.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Onkar Bhujbal, and this video is about why A.I. pipelines silently degrade. In traditional software, a function that adds two numbers today will still add them tomorrow. But when you wrap an application around a large language model, a change in model version, a reworded system prompt, or a shift in upstream data can break your downstream architecture — without anyone touching your code.

output: Your code: unchanged. Your dependency: a model.
A model is a dependency that updates without a version bump.

beats.honesty_note: No accuracy figure, decay rate or model is named — the script reports none. The hook describes the failure CLASS the script describes, not a measured incident on this project.

beats.narration_text: You cannot test what a model will say. You can test everything you built around it — and you can make the repository refuse code that breaks it. That is the whole of continuous integration for A.I.

beats.authoring_note: fontSize raised to 92 (earlier reels used 52-58). At 4K two short lines at 54px filled only ~5% of the safe area and GATE V flagged `underfill` on every previous reel's final. Short text here keeps it inside the title-safe width at 92.

beats.narration_text: Testing A.I. is fundamentally different from testing standard code. You cannot assert that a model's output will precisely match a hardcoded string. Instead you test the deterministic guardrails that surround it. Continuous integration for A.I. means continuously testing your parsers, your normalizers and your fail-safes against a suite of known adversarial inputs.

stages.name: DYNAMIC INFERENCE

beats.narration_text: This is where a continuous integration pipeline — something like GitHub Actions — stops being a nicety. A C.I. pipeline is an automated robot living in your repository. Every time an engineer tries to update the system, it rebuilds the application in a vacuum and fires malicious data at it, before a human ever sees the change.

beats.narration_text: So let's watch what happens when someone deletes a security check and tries to merge it anyway. This is the moment the whole pipeline is for.
beats.new_visual_element: Ask micro-beat — the prompt that runs the failing PR

show.event: composer already framed; the prompt types in
running indicator reads 'running the check suite…'; no output lines — the next beat IS the output

props.command: A pull request removes one regex from the sanitizer. Run the suite and show me whether the merge button is reachable.

beats.authoring_note: ASK → RESULT pair: BASK is the ask, B04 is the result (ASK→RESULT LAW).

beats.narration_text: If a developer accidentally removes a security regex, or a new model update starts slipping past the evaluation logic, the pipeline catches it in isolation. It locks the repository and stops the compromised code from reaching production. That is the difference between hoping your guardrails held and knowing they did.
beats.new_visual_element: The diff that broke it, beside the merge button that will not arm

show.event: left panel lands: the one-line diff that removed the check
right panel lands: PULL REQUEST #58 · GitHub Actions
check counter climbs, then STOPS short of the total
the button stays MERGE BLOCKED — it never arms
blocked state holds through the cut

beats.honesty_note: PR #58 and the 41-of-64 check counts are ILLUSTRATIVE — the script supplies no real numbers, and this is a generic teaching example rather than a run on any repository. The counter deliberately stops short of the total so the merge button never arms, which is the beat's claim.

beats.narration_text: So never assume your guardrails will survive the next commit. Build an automated integration pipeline that aggressively attacks your own system on every update — and make a failing attack block the merge.

show.event: code card opens on a hard cut; traffic-light dot arms terracotta
the workflow reveals line by line
the TASK line lands: automate your regression tests
the branch-protection note lands last — the part people skip

props.title: .github/workflows/ci.yml
props.code:
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  attack:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: pytest tests/adversarial -v

# TASK: automate your regression tests.

# Then the step everyone skips:
#   mark this check REQUIRED in branch
#   protection. A red X nobody has to
#   obey is just a suggestion.

beats.authoring_note: The branch-protection comment is the reel's addition. A CI job that reports failure but is not marked required does not block anything — the script's Scene 4 claim ('physically locks the repository') is only true with that setting on.

beats.narration_text: And here is the prompt worth running before you trust any of it. Hand a model your test suite and ask which of your guardrails it could break without a single test going red. The gap between what you test and what you rely on is where the next regression is already living.

beats.narration_text: Your model will change under you. Your tests are the only thing that notices. Onkar Bhujbal, for Humanitarians AI.
